```{r setup}
#| include: false
source("theme.R")
```

We introduce `housepi`, a package for the study of epidemiological data from household outbreaks.
In this vignette we'll walk through the process of loading a model, associating necessary definitions to perform inference and simulations.

# The housepi model class

The central element of the package is the class `HousepiModel`, an [R6 class](https://r6.r-lib.org/articles/Introduction.html), used to wrap an Rcpp environment.
We show how to generate a new instance of such a class with a template model, the chain binomial:

```{r}
# import the library 'housepi'
library(housepi)
# set general seed
set.seed(42)

# generate an instance of the chain binomial model
hhmodel <- new_housepi_model("chain_binomial")
```

At any moment we can retrieve the template model description by using the method `$help()`.

## A collection of household models

To see the complete list of available template models, from within Rstudio just run

```{r}
# present the list of template model name
template_household_model()
```

Each template comes with its template definitions that can be used straight away or changed.
To know more about each model, choose a name from the previous list and run, e.
g.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# show model description in RStudio help window
template_household_model("chain_binomial")
```

This command will open the relative documentation file in the Help window of your Rstudio session.
Our project aims at expanding the present collection of templates, in order to foster off-the-shelf analysis.

## Format of the data

Data can be provided as a numerical data.frame in wide format, where individual information are organised by row.
Individuals with tagged with the same `"house_id"` in the respective column are considered to belong to same household.
Additionally, an individual identifier `"id"` can be provided within the respective column.

To perform model inference, a `"status"` must be provided for each individual $i$.
Status $s_{i}$ should be an integer value satisfying the following convention:

| Status $s_{i}$      | Compartment | Serology     |
|:-------------------:|-------------|--------------|
| $\geq$ `1`          | infectious  | seropositive |
| `0`                 | susceptible | seronegative |
| $\leq$ `-1` or `NA` | missing     | missing      |

## Data importation

The most direct way to associate a data to a model is assigning it to the active method `$data_wide`.
The `housepi` package comes with a few public datasets to be used for testing.

```{r}
# import data in wide format using R6 active field
hhmodel$data_wide <- housepi::survey
```
alternatively, we can use the call `add_data_wide()`, as shown later in this walkthrough. 
We can extract summary information about current loaded data with `summarise_cases()`:

```{r}
# show a summary of cases as a `flextable`
summarise_cases(hhmodel) |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::theme_vanilla() |>
  flextable::set_formatter(pct = function(x) round(x, 1)) |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = ~ type) |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ type + comment, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::labelizor(labels = c(type = "", comment = "", pct = "[%]")) |>
  flextable::bg(bg = "white", part = "all") |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 12, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

To learn more about `flextable` objects and how to export or format them, see [flextable](https://cloud.r-project.org/web/packages/flextable/).

At any moment we can export the loaded data by invoking the method `$data_wide`.

## Associate parameter definitions

Here we show how to provide a single parameter definition (prior and proposal needed for the Bayesian Monte Carlo).
Different approaches are available to perform the same operation, we can call `add_parameter()` or invoke the namesake R6 method:

```{r}
# alpha : community transmission rate
hhmodel <- hhmodel |>
  add_parameter("alpha",                # name matching the model source
                prior = "uniform",      # uniform prior
                proposal = "lognormal") # mcmc proposal

# beta : in-household person to person transmission rate
hhmodel$add_parameter("beta", prior = "uniform", proposal = "lognormal")
```

At any moment we can turn a parameter definition into a constant definition: it is sufficient to set the argument `const = TRUE` (in such case a `value` must be provided).

For further information on the available options for the definition of the parameter priors and MCMC proposal, see the vignette [Bayesian MCMC options](bayesian_mcmc_options.html).

# Perform inference

After having provided all necessary definitions, we can perform inference calling `run_inference()`.
Standard options for the Monte Carlo Markov chain can be provided at this stage, including controls on the number of threads^[Multi-threading is implemented with *openMP* which is unfortunately not supported on latest macOS distributions.
The option `threads` is disabled on such systems.] and on the progress bar.
This will return an object wrapping [posterior](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/posterior/) `draws` objects that can be accessed to compute estimates.

```{r}
# run the Monte Carlo specifying setup options
results <- hhmodel |>
  run_inference(steps = 1000,     # number of mcmc steps (per chain)
                thin = 10,        # delay between mcmc steps that are stored
                adapt = 500,      # finite adaptation steps before mcmc steps
                chains = 3,       # number of independent chains
                threads = 1,      # number of threads
                progress = FALSE) # disable progress bar

# summarize posterior draws of parameters
posterior::summarize_draws(get_param_draws(results))
```

We can proceed as usual with other popolar R packages for Bayesian analysis.
For example, we can extract the parameters draws by calling `get_param_draws` and plot traces with [bayesplot](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bayesplot/)

```{r}
#| fig.alt: 
#|  Trace plots for alpha and beta parameters across MCMC iterations with three parallel chains overlaid.
# visualize the traces of the first chain with 'bayesplot'
get_param_draws(results) |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace(facet_args = list(ncol = 1))
```

or to perform model comparison, we can call functions from [loo](https://cloud.r-project.org/web/packages/loo/).
We can extract the sample of pointwise log-likelihood for each household and compute for example the leave-one-out cross-validation as follows

```{r}
# LOO-CV (leave-one-out cross-validation)
get_log_lik_draws(results) |>
  posterior::as_draws_matrix() |>
  loo::loo()
```

# Augment infection times

For models requiring augmented variables, the definition procedure is analogous.
In [Data augmentation](data_augmentation.html) we broadly discuss data augmentation and the process of more complex augmented definitions.
Here we present a case sttudy, using the template model "augm-infection-time" where surveys are conditioned on single introduction.
We load the parameter definitions directly from the model template.

```{r}
hhsimul <- new_housepi_model("augmented_infection_time") |>
  load_parameter_template()

# inspect parameter definitions
get_parameters(hhsimul)
```

## Simulate an outbreak

We propose the following definitions for the augmented variables, 
associated from a list by calling `load_augmented_list()`.

```{r}
hhsimul <- hhsimul |>
  load_augmented_list(
    # define default infection times of primary cases
    # secondary infection times are taken care by the simulation
    infec_time = list(model = "lognormal",
                      meanlog = 4, sdlog = 0.5, max = 365),
    
    # define an incubation period for each individual
    # arguments are linked to parameters
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma",
                        shape = ~ inc_shape@P, scale = ~ inc_scale@P,
                        max = 14),
    
    # define 'onset_time' as the sum of incubation period and infection time
    onset_time = ~ infec_time + incub_period
  )
```

When dealing with many different nested definitions it is not usual to loose track of which definition are missing. 
We can inspect the state of the current loaded model definitions just by printing the model:

```{r}
# print current state of definitions 
hhsimul

# append missing parameters for incubation period
hhsimul <- hhsimul |> 
  load_parameter_list(
    inc_shape = 2, inc_scale = 1.1,
    # we set option 'append' to TRUE to keep previous definitions
    append = TRUE 
  )
```
To see how to associate group rates in heterogeneous models, see the vignette [Group rates](group_rates.html).
However, by default if no group rate definition is provided all values are set to reference value 1, so we can forget about this alert for the rest of the walkthrough.

We then run a simulation with the method `run_simulation`, using the same community structure from the survey, but dropping cases.
In this configuration, introductions are sampled randomly. 
Simulation will associated augmented incubation periods and onset times in addition to status.
We then propose a simple observation process, where we assume onsets after 6 PM (18/24) are reported to next day. We also want to drop unobserved quantities. We can do both by assigning such a function to the argument `observation`:

```{r}
simulated <- hhsimul |>
  add_data_wide(dplyr::mutate(housepi::survey, status = NA)) |>
  run_simulation(obs_process = function(x) {
    x$onset_date <- ifelse(x$status > 0, floor(x$onset_time + 0.25), NA)
    x$incub_period <- x$onset_time <- x$infec_time <- NULL
    x
  })

head(simulated)
```

## Validate the approach with a simulation study

We can check that inference returns the parameters used for the simulation.

```{r}
hhmodel <- hhsimul |>
  # loading definitions from list drops previous by default
  load_augmented_list(
    infec_time = ~ onset_time - incub_period,
    onset_time = list(model = "normal", mean = ~ onset_date@D, sd = 1),
    incub_period = list(model = "gamma",
                        shape = ~ inc_shape@P, scale = ~ inc_scale@P)
  )

results <- hhmodel |>
  add_data_wide(simulated) |>
  run_inference(chains = 3, steps = 1000, adapt = 500, thin = 10,
                # update progress bar every 3 seconds
                progress = 3)
```
We can visualize traces vs expected values as follows

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.alt: >
#|  Trace plots for alpha, beta, and gamma parameters with three chains.
#|  Overlaying orange lines indicate the values used for the simulation.
library(ggplot2)

# extract sample to posterioir::draws_df
param_draws <- get_param_draws(results)

# select original parameters used for the simulation
simul_parameters <- get_parameters(hhsimul) |>
  dplyr::select(name, value) |> 
  dplyr::filter(name %in% posterior::variables(param_draws)) |> 
  dplyr::rename(parameter = name, simulated = value)

# use bayesplot to plot the posterior draws
bayesplot::mcmc_trace(param_draws, facet_args = list(ncol = 1)) +
  geom_hline(data = simul_parameters, aes(yintercept = simulated))
```

```{r}
#| fig.width: 5
#| fig.height: 2.5
#| fig.alt: >
#|  R-hat convergence diagnostics for alpha, beta, and gamma parameters with color-coded thresholds.
#|  Color intensity represents R-hat values (≤1.05, ≤1.1, >1.1). Points near 1.0 indicate convergence.
# compute Rhat values associate to inferred parameters
var_names <- get_parameters(hhmodel) |>
  dplyr::filter(!const) |>
  dplyr::pull(name)
rhat_values <- sapply(var_names, function(v) posterior::rhat(param_draws[[v]]))

# use bayesplot to showcase Rhat statistics
bayesplot::mcmc_rhat(rhat_values) +
  bayesplot::yaxis_text(hjust = 1)
```

Here we performed R-hat diagnostics computing the values of $\hat{R}$ with [posterior](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/posterior/).

Finally we wrap all together to compare to parameters used for simulation.

```{r}
posterior::summarise_draws(param_draws) |>
  dplyr::reframe(parameter = variable,
                 inferred = format_credible_intervals(mean, q5, q95)) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(simul_parameters, by = "parameter") |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::separate_header() |>
  flextable::theme_vanilla() |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ parameter, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::bg(bg = "white", part = "all") |>
  flextable::fontsize(size = 12, part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

Due to the stochastic nature of this kind of simulation, limiting to re-infer parameters is a limiting check. 
In [Posterior predictive checks](posterior_predictive_checks.html) we show how to compute common household measures according to the model posterior distribution.
